summary:
AURA-5 is an onboard "fifth crew member" designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. The main challenge is that astronauts may experience medical symptoms, sleep loss, stress, isolation, fatigue, or reduced readiness while being far from immediate medical assistance and facing communication delays with Earth.
AURA-5 is designed to collect daily health records from the astronaut's suit, smartwatch, wearable sensors, and onboard assessments, including vital signs, sleep, nutrition, hydration, mood, stress, cognitive performance, and previous complaints. When an astronaut reports a concern, the system reviews their personal history and baseline and prepares a clear report for the appropriate medical or psychological support team on Earth.
The system supports sleep, mental health, crew relationships, symptom reporting through a body model, focus testing before critical tasks, and task reassignment when an astronaut is not ready. In dangerous situations, AURA-5 gives spoken emergency instructions; the full system will also alert nearby crew and support the response if the astronaut cannot respond. Our working prototype demonstrates this journey using simulated mission data and simulated ground links. AURA-5 turns health records into timely action, so no astronaut is left without support.
details:
During long-duration missions, physical symptoms, inadequate sleep, demanding workloads, isolation, and psychological stress can interact. Astronauts may need to recognize changes in their health while continuing to perform complex tasks, sometimes without immediate guidance from Earth. NASA explains that Mars communication delays can range from approximately four to 24 minutes in each direction. A question and its reply therefore cannot be assumed to arrive in real time.

AURA-5 explores how a single visual interface could help crew members gather relevant observations, identify reasons for concern, follow structured next steps, and prepare a readable medical handoff. The intended contribution is the complete user journey, not a claim that software can independently replace a flight surgeon.

Daily health records and personal context

The prototype includes a synthetic mission dataset representing four crew members over 180 days. Its dashboard displays pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and temperature. Selected indicators are compared with personal baselines derived from the first 14 simulated mission days, alongside multi-day trends.

Morning and evening check-ins record information such as sleep, alertness, mood, stress, workload, loneliness, meals, hydration, caffeine, and team-related concerns. These observations provide context for the interface's explanations and support suggestions; they are not proof of a medical condition.

Users can manually enter vital signs. Source labels distinguish simulated values (SIM), manually entered values (MANUAL), and measurements from attention sessions played in the browser (REAL). A REAL label on a reaction-time result does not mean that the result came from a flight-certified sensor or a validated clinical assessment.

In the proposed future system, compatible sensors, smart garments, and other certified devices could supply measurements automatically. The present prototype does not continuously collect data from an astronaut's suit, smartwatch, or wearable sensors.

Symptoms, safety questions, and explainable urgency

When a user reports a concern, the interactive schematic body model helps identify the location of discomfort. The user can select symptoms, answer focused danger-sign questions, and review the information supporting the displayed urgency category.

The rule-based assessment uses green, yellow, stronger-yellow, and red categories. Physiological observations and danger signs guide urgency, while sleep, stress, and attention can add context. The design keeps danger-sign assessment separate from general wellbeing: reassuring sleep or stress information must not be treated as evidence that an urgent physical warning is safe.

Follow-up and remeasurement workflows record additional observations and can escalate a case. These categories and thresholds are prototype rules, not an approved spacecraft medical protocol. Selected NEWS2 physiological bands inform the implementation, but AURA-5 is not a complete or certified NEWS2 assessment.

Sleep, psychological support, and crew wellbeing

AURA-5 includes guidance for sleep difficulties and supportive prompts for stress, mood changes, loneliness, and interpersonal strain. Features include breathing guidance, journaling, and suggestions for routines and social connection.

These features are intended to encourage reflection and appropriate human support. They do not provide psychotherapy, diagnose a psychological disorder, or establish a connection with a psychologist. Requests and responses involving support teams are simulated.

The Silent Hour

When a case is rated red, AURA-5 starts a Silent Hour workflow built around the Mars communication delay. A summary of symptoms, vital signs, personal baseline and sleep context is prepared and sent to Earth automatically after a short countdown (simulated in the prototype). While the crew waits, the system speaks first-aid steps one at a time and waits for the astronaut to say "done", repeats measurements every five minutes, logs every action with its time, and shows a timer for the earliest possible reply: 24 minutes out, ground review, and 24 minutes back. The ground review time of 45 minutes is our own assumption. First-aid steps cover 27 symptoms across 25 body regions and are based on the IFRC 2020 first aid guidelines. No drug or dose is ever suggested.

Focus check and crew readiness

Before a high-risk task, the astronaut first rates how alert they feel and then plays a three-minute reaction-time task inspired by PVT-B research. AURA-5 compares the felt and the measured result with the astronaut's own baseline. If focus is reduced, it suggests giving the task to a more ready crewmate; the commander decides. Crewmates see readiness only, not the health reasons behind it. A lighter plan for the next day is suggested when someone is worn out.

Voice and languages

A complaint can be reported by voice, touch or typing. The system repeats what it understood and asks for confirmation before assessing. The whole interface, including the spoken guidance, works in English and Arabic. Speech features depend on the browser.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

For the crew: a clear next step at any moment, including when Earth cannot answer in time. For the ground team: an early notice of every case, at every level, with a readable summary instead of scattered readings. Our vision for the full system is automatic readings from suit and wearable sensors, alerts to nearby crew when an astronaut cannot respond, speech understood on board without a network, and thresholds validated by flight surgeons on real crews. The same approach could serve remote clinics, ships and polar stations on Earth. These vision features are not in the current prototype.

How the project is creative and what we considered

AURA-5 is designed as a nurse, not a doctor: it assesses, guides and reports, and never diagnoses. Sleep, mood and focus are treated as early signals alongside vital signs, so one health event is not seen in isolation. The focus check compares what the astronaut feels with what is measured before the task is assigned. We considered safety first (a red warning can never be lowered by good sleep or mood data), privacy inside a small crew, honesty about simulated data, and the lack of public daily health records of astronauts, which was our biggest challenge and the reason all sensor data are synthetic and labelled.

Tools

Python (Flask, Jinja), SQLite, HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with the browser Web Speech API for voice. Hosted on Replit. The code was written with Claude (Anthropic) from the team's descriptions and corrections and deployed with Replit Agent; the logo is an AI-generated image (ChatGPT). Decisions inside the product come from written rules, not from an AI model.
